headline: Four Valparaíso ascensores worth an afternoon, and what each one costs at the window
article_markdown:
Valparaíso built about thirty hill lifts from 1883 onward. Sixteen structures survive, and seven carry passengers. That is the number to plan around: the ascensores are still working transit for people who live above the flat, they cost pocket change, and half an afternoon is enough to ride three or four of them properly.

**What you pay.** Since 2 January 2026 the municipal fare table reads: 200 pesos general, 300 pesos on Concepción, 600 pesos for a bicycle on Barón or Cordillera, and 1,000 pesos for foreign tourists. The split is nationality, not neighbourhood. A Chilean down from Santiago pays 200 and a foreign visitor pays 1,000 for the same forty-second ride. The tourist surcharge is not new; it was introduced in 2019 at 700 pesos and raised in January. Under-14s, students with a valid credential and over-60s are listed as exempt, though the published notice does not say whether foreign visitors qualify, and it does not say whether the 1,000-peso rate replaces or stacks against Concepción's 300. Carry coins for 1,000 per ride each way and expect change. I could not confirm whether any window takes cards.

**El Peral, first.** The lower station is on Plaza de la Justicia, beside Plaza Sotomayor, so it is the easiest one to find if you have just walked in from the port. Foreign fare 1,000 pesos, published hours 07:00 to 21:30. You step out at Paseo Yugoslavo on Cerro Alegre, a railed walkway with the port cranes, Cerro Cordillera, Artillería and Playa Ancha laid out below and the financial blocks directly underneath. Palacio Baburizza is right there, holding the municipal fine arts collection: Tuesday to Sunday, 10:30 to 18:00, 11,000 pesos general, which is more than ten rides. If you want to sit, sit inside the museum or at a café along the paseo. I found no source confirming public benches on Yugoslavo itself, and the walkway reads as a standing viewpoint.

**Concepción, downhill.** Walk the ten minutes east from Yugoslavo along the Cerro Alegre and Cerro Concepción paseos and you arrive at Paseo Gervasoni, the top station of the oldest ascensor in the city, running since 1883. Published hours 07:00 to 21:30, general fare 300 pesos, foreign fare posted at 1,000. Gervasoni is a wrought-iron-railed balcony over the bay with the Museo Mirador Lukas, a house museum of the cartoonist Renzo Pecchenino, at its western end a few metres from the station. Seating here is commercial: the café terraces along the paseo, not municipal benches. Ride it down to Calle Prat and you are back on the flat among the old banking buildings, which is the point of taking it in that direction.

**Reina Victoria, back up.** From Prat, head east to Calle Elías near Plaza Aníbal Pinto. Foreign fare 1,000 pesos, published hours 07:00 to 21:30. The car climbs to Paseo Dimalow on Cerro Alegre in well under a minute, arriving in the middle of the mural-covered stretch most visitors photograph. One caveat that affects what you will find up there: the municipality awarded a 157-million-peso repair of the Dimalow walkway and mirador, rebuilding railings, stairs and handrails, with work starting in April 2026 on a 180-day programme run in two phases so that pedestrians and the ascensor keep moving. Shops and bars along the paseo are reported to be trading normally. Assume part of the viewpoint, and whatever seating sits on it, may be fenced when you arrive. The terraces are the dependable place to sit.

**Cordillera, if you still have an hour.** Lower station on Calle Serrano in Barrio Puerto, upper station on Plaza Eleuterio Ramírez. Foreign fare 1,000 pesos, published hours 07:00 to 21:30, 600 pesos if you bring a bicycle. This is the least touristed of the four and the most residential: a small square with the 1842 Casa Lord Cochrane on it, views back over Plaza Sotomayor and the historic quarters. Treat the house as scenery rather than a plan. Reports describe it as no longer functioning as a museum, with its collection moved and access unclear, so do not build the trip around getting inside. The square is public and you can walk down the 162 steps of the Cienfuegos staircase alongside the track instead of paying for the return.

The other three runners, if these are shut or you arrive elsewhere: Barón, which lands beside Avenida Diego Portales and is the obvious first ride if you come from Viña del Mar on the train; Espíritu Santo on Cerro Bellavista, for the open-air mural museum; and San Agustín in Barrio Puerto, which closes earlier, at 21:00.

**The dead ones.** By 2024 reporting, Valparaíso had fifteen ascensores in the public inventory and seven working, against fifteen all running in 2003. Polanco has been out since 2024 and remains in restoration and redesign. Artillería has been stopped since 2021, with contract award for its repair scheduled only for 31 August 2026. Villaseca and Monjas have sat at roughly sixty per cent of a restoration that stalled in 2019. Florida, Mariposas and Lecheros are out, Lecheros since a fire in 2007. Ownership is split between the municipality and the regional government, which is a large part of why the faults, described as mechanical rather than structural, take years.

**Status and hours, honestly.** The seven-operating list was last verified publicly on 22 May 2026; I checked for closures on 7 September 2026 and found none reported, but no source verifies same-day operation, and individual cars go out for maintenance without notice. Published network hours are 07:00 to 21:30 weekdays and 08:00 to 21:30 weekends and holidays, listed as a winter schedule. Hours will not constrain an afternoon; a single closed gate might, so keep the parallel staircase in mind at each one.
